title: Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters
source: Axios — Why the world's biggest climate meeting (still) matters (2026-11-17)
body: Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else. Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone. "The fact that in these very disruptive times on trade and multilateralism, two wars going on, and inflation everywhere, countries can come together and actually prioritize this is a very important point," said Ani Dasgupta, head of the World Resources Institute. Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change. A first draft of a potential agreement released Monday includes proposals to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and electrify more of the global economy. But countries remain divided over what should make the final cut. Arab countries and Russia are pushing back against proposals on fossil fuels and electrification, while the European Union is backing the electrification goal but demanding substantial changes to the broader agreement, according to Climate Home News . If the past is prologue, we'll probably see some kind of deal emerge hours or a couple days after Friday's scheduled conclusion, given these meetings' habit of running overtime. The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress. Projected warming by 2100 has actually dropped from roughly 3.5 degrees to 2.7 degrees, according to Climate Action Tracker — still far above the Paris goal, but considerably less than previously feared. But progress has stalled since 2020, as rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel development and government policy reversals offset gains in clean energy. "The past decade demonstrates both what climate policy can achieve and the consequences of inaction," states Climate Action Tracker's latest report, issued in Turkey. State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities. A warming world is already affecting virtually all of us, probably in ways we don't think about most of the time — whether it's wildfire smoke, higher insurance premiums or, you know, hotter weather. Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer. Homeowners in areas that face greater wildfire and wind risks generally pay higher insurance premiums, according to a Government Accountability Office report published earlier this year. Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick: An AI revolution happening faster than most of us can process, other than that it might end our jobs — or humanity. A real-life spy and affair scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that seems pulled straight from Hollywood. Wars and geopolitical turmoil that have sent energy prices soaring. And, of course, there's affordability, which dominated this month's U.S. elections, including among victorious Democrats who didn't emphasize climate change . Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed. By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly. Over the next two years, respondents ranked economic confrontation between countries as the biggest risk, with extreme weather, worsened by climate change, in fourth place. Over the next decade, extreme weather topped the list, followed by biodiversity loss and critical changes to Earth's systems. How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police. This year's attendance is dwarfing prior years and approaching 100,000, according to United Nations and Bloomberg News data. Official government negotiations are at the center, producing agreements that influence domestic policies and investments. Surrounding them are increasingly crowded circles of events, from trade shows to protests, where you often capture the zeitgeist of each year's confab. Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification. Organizers launched a voluntary pledge Monday to make AI more climate-friendly, including encouraging cleaner electricity and greater transparency about data centers' environmental impacts. The initiative I mentioned earlier aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from roughly 23% to 35% by 2035. Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic. In 2024, prominent climate leaders, including former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, called for a major overhaul focused more on implementing existing promises. Even the UN's top climate official, Simon Stiell, acknowledged Saturday that the process needs to evolve. "Can the process be better optimized? Absolutely," he said. Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year. Yet the Trump administration is sitting it out for the second straight year, and the leaders of China and India skipped it, sending lower-level officials instead. Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey). Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement. Many reporters, including myself, spent much of the time asking officials whether they thought newly elected President Trump would really withdraw from the deal like he promised on the campaign trail. Boy, were we naive back then. In Dubai in 2023, an oil-rich country hosting a climate conference drew predictable criticism. Yet that COP produced the first global agreement calling for a transition away from fossil fuels. The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.
